extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, political economists, educators, and institutional reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and standards for when joint-stock companies are appropriate and for the organization, incentives, and discipline of educational institutions and teachers. The guidance covers what trades suit corporate organization, necessary conditions for such establishments, and how funding/authority shapes teacher behaviour and student outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of joint-stock companies to routine trades
rubrics_metrics.description: The only trades which it seems possible for a joint-stock company to carry on successfully, without an exclusive privilege, are those, of which all the operations are capable of being reduced to what is called a routine, or to such a uniformity of method as admits of little or no variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: banking, insurance (fire/sea/capture), making and maintaining a navigable cut or canal, and bringing water for the supply of a great city. Emphasis on operations reducible to strict rule and method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banking trade fit for joint-stock management
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles of the banking trade... the practice is capable of being reduced to strict rules. Such companies, therefore, seem extremely well fitted for this trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that departure from strict rules for speculative gain is dangerous. Joint-stock companies are described as generally more tenacious of established rules than private copartneries. Examples: principal banking companies in Europe; Bank of England's limited exclusive privilege; Edinburgh banks as joint-stock without exclusive privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance trade fit for joint-stock management
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of the risk, either from fire, or from loss by sea, or by capture... admits... of such a gross estimation, as renders it, in some degree, reducible to strict rule and method. The trade of insurance, therefore, may be carried on successfully by a joint-stock company, without any exclusive privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: London Assurance and Royal Exchange Assurance companies have no such exclusive privilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canals and waterworks fit for joint-stock management
rubrics_metrics.description: When a navigable cut or canal has been once made, the management of it becomes quite simple and easy, and it is reducible to strict rule and method. Even the making of it is so, as it may be contracted for with undertakers, at so much a mile, and so much a lock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same holds for aqueducts and large pipes supplying a city; such undertakings frequently are successfully managed by joint-stock companies without exclusive privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two necessary conditions beyond routineness for reasonable joint-stock establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: To render such an establishment perfectly reasonable... two other circumstances ought to concur. First, it ought to appear with the clearest evidence, that the undertaking is of greater and more general utility than the greater part of common trades; and, secondly, that it requires a greater capital than can easily be collected into a private copartnery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If moderate capital suffices, even great utility alone is not sufficient reason for forming a joint-stock company because private adventurers would supply demand. In the four named trades both circumstances concur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly often necessary for joint-stock companies in foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a monopoly, however, a joint-stock company... cannot long carry on any branch of foreign trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: private adventurers' superior vigilance and attention usually outcompete corporations in dynamic foreign-trade warfare; monopolies were historically used to sustain such companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint-stock companies prone to failure from mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Many joint-stock companies for foreign trade... have all failed from mismanagement, notwithstanding they had exclusive privileges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference to historical lists (Abbe Morellet) and counter-examples; caution that exclusive privilege does not guarantee success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazards of joint-stock companies created to promote particular manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint-stock companies, which are established for the public-spirited purpose of promoting some particular manufacture... can, in other respects, scarce ever fail to do more harm than good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: unavoidable partiality of directors to particular branches, being misled by undertakers, discouraging other manufacturers and disturbing the natural proportion between industry and profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional funding (endowments) diminishes teacher's necessity of application
rubrics_metrics.description: The endowments of schools and colleges have necessarily diminished, more or less, the necessity of application in the teachers. Their subsistence, so far as it arises from their salaries, is evidently derived from a fund, altogether independent of their success and reputation in their particular professions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where teacher income depends primarily on fees from pupils, the necessity for application remains greater; salaried positions reduce incentives to exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher exertion proportional to necessity to make exertion
rubrics_metrics.description: In every profession, the exertion of the greater part of those who exercise it, is always in proportion to the necessity they are under of making that exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competition and necessity (e.g., to earn subsistence) motivate diligence; great objects alone without necessity rarely produce sustained exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary-only remuneration sets teacher's interest against duty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reward of the master... his salary constitutes the whole of the revenue which he derives from his office. His interest is, in this case, set as directly in opposition to his duty... it is certainly his interest... either to neglect it altogether, or... to perform it in as careless and slovenly a manner as that authority will permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with teachers who also receive pupil fees and thus retain incentive via reputation and gratitude of pupils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal collegiate authority fosters collusion and indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the authority to which he is subject resides in the body corporate, the college, or university, of which he himself is a member... they are likely to make a common cause, to be all very indulgent to one another, and every man to consent that his neighbour may neglect his duty, provided he himself is allowed to neglect his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to diminished teaching effort; example: many Oxford public professors have given up the pretence of teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: External (extraneous) authority is arbitrary and degrades teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: If the authority to which he is subject resides, not so much in the body corporate... as in some other extraneous persons... it is not... very likely that he will be suffered to neglect his duty altogether. All that such superiors, however, can force him to do, is to attend upon his pupils a certain number of hours... What those lectures shall be, must still depend upon the diligence of the teacher; and that diligence is likely to be proportioned to the motives which he has for exerting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraneous jurisdiction is liable to be exercised ignorantly and capriciously; it degrades the teacher and encourages obsequiousness rather than genuine merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forcing students to institutions reduces emulation and teacher merit incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever forces a certain number of students to any college or university, independent of the merit or reputation of the teachers, tends more or less to diminish the necessity of that merit or reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Privileges of graduates and charitable foundations attach students to institutions independent of teacher merit; allowing free choice could stimulate emulation among colleges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on changing tutors reduce emulation and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: If in each college, the tutor or teacher... should not be voluntarily chosen by the student, but appointed by the head of the college; and if... the student should not be allowed to change him for another, without leave... such a regulation would... extinguish all emulation among the different tutors... and to diminish very much, in all of them, the necessity of diligence and of attention to their respective pupils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Student choice of tutor and ease of changing tutor are implied mechanisms to maintain teacher diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers can deliver sham lectures when incentives are weak
rubrics_metrics.description: The teacher, instead of explaining to his pupils himself the science... may read some book upon it; and... by making them interpret it to him, and by now and then making an occasional remark upon it, he may flatter himself that he is giving a lecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline can enforce attendance for such sham lectures, masking poor teaching rather than improving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: College discipline primarily for masters' ease rather than student benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: The discipline of colleges and universities is in general contrived, not for the benefit of the students, but for the interest, or... for the ease of the masters. Its object is, in all cases, to maintain the authority of the master...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where masters perform their duty, students rarely neglect theirs; genuine quality of lectures obviates need for coercive discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good lectures remove need for coercive attendance after early adolescence
rubrics_metrics.description: No discipline is ever requisite to force attendance upon lectures which are really worth the attending... after twelve or thirteen years of age, provided the master does his duty, force or restraint can scarce ever be necessary to carry on any part of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Force may be suitable for very young children only; for older students, quality of instruction should motivate attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private instruction often better for practical skills; schools less corrupted than universities
rubrics_metrics.description: Those parts of education, it is to be observed, for the teaching of which there are no public institutions, are generally the best taught... In England, the public schools are much less corrupted than the universities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical skills (fencing, dancing, basic literacy and numeracy) are commonly acquired in private settings and seldom fail to be learned; structural differences in reward systems help explain variation in teaching quality.
